About
Faculty of Agriculture, Food and Environment
Hebrew University of Jerusalem — Rehovot Campus
Welcome to the Agrotech-lab course, where you will have the opportunity to learn about the integration of microcontrollers in agriculture technology. In this course, you will explore the use of microcontrollers such as the ESP32 and how they can be utilized to automate processes, collect data, and improve overall efficiency in agricultural practices.
Throughout the course, you will gain practical knowledge on how to design, develop, and implement microcontroller-based solutions for different applications in agriculture. You will learn how to use sensors to collect data such as temperature, humidity, and soil moisture, and how to integrate this data with the ESP32 to automate irrigation systems, monitor plant growth, and more.
This course is designed for students who are interested in the application of technology in agriculture and want to gain hands-on experience in designing and implementing microcontroller-based solutions. By the end of this course, you will have a solid understanding of how to apply microcontrollers in agricultural practices, which will equip you with valuable skills for future research or professional opportunities.

title: 1  Arduino intro
text:
1.1 What is a microcontroller?
Welcome to the world of microcontrollers! In this course, we will be exploring the fascinating world of microcontrollers and how they can be used to control electronic devices.
A microcontroller, also known as an MCU, is a tiny computer that is capable of performing a variety of tasks. It is a single metal-oxide-semiconductor (MOS) integrated circuit (IC) chip that contains one or more central processing units (CPUs), memory, and programmable input/output peripherals. The MCU can receive input from various sensors and devices, process that input, and provide an output to control other devices.

title: 1  Arduino intro
text:
1.2 Arduino
One popular brand of microcontrollers is Arduino. Arduino is a company that produces user-friendly microcontroller boards, such as the Arduino Uno, Arduino Mega, and Arduino Nano. These boards are widely used and have extensive documentation and online resources available. The Arduino board contains a microcontroller chip, memory, and input/output pins that can be used to interface with other electronic components such as sensors, motors, LEDs, and displays.
The Arduino board can be programmed using a simplified version of the C++ programming language, which makes it accessible for beginners to learn and use. The board is also open-source, meaning that anyone can access and modify the hardware and software designs.

title: 1  Arduino intro
text:
1.3 Applications
Arduino is being used for a wide variety of applications, including home automation, robotics, environmental monitoring, and education. For instance, Arduino can be used to control lights, fans, and other appliances in a home automation system. It is popular among hobbyists and students for building robots and automated systems. Lastly, Arduino is widely used to monitor temperature, humidity, and other environmental factors for research or industrial applications.

title: 1  Arduino intro
text:
1.4 ESP32 = Arduino\(^2\) + WiFi + Bluetooth
However, in this course, we will not be using Arduino boards. Instead, we will be using the ESP32 microcontroller (to be exact, the FIreBeetle 2 ESP32 board), which is similar to Arduino in terms of its programming environment, but has additional features such as built-in WiFi and Bluetooth capabilities. This makes it ideal for internet of things (IoT) projects and wireless communication. The ESP32 is also affordable, with boards costing around $5 each.
Throughout this course, you will learn how to program the ESP32 to control various electronic devices. You will learn how to interface the ESP32 with sensors, motors, displays, and other devices. By the end of this course, you will have the skills and knowledge to create your own custom microcontroller projects.
So get ready to dive into the exciting world of microcontrollers with the ESP32!

title: VS Code + PlatformIO
text:
What changes from Arduino IDE?
An optional workflow for students who want to take their projects further. We will use the FireBeetle 2 ESP32-E, keep programming with Arduino functions, and put the code, board settings, libraries, and an optional AI assistant in one workspace.
By the end, you will have a blinking LED, messages in the Serial Monitor, and a project you can share with a teammate. Start with steps 1–5; the later sections help you move an existing sketch and work on larger projects.
Checked: October 19, 2026. Menus may move as the extensions change. The links throughout this guide go to the official documentation.
You are changing the tools on your computer. The board still runs your program, and setup(), loop(), digitalWrite(), and the other Arduino functions still work when you select the Arduino framework.
Arduino IDE remains a convenient way to start. Modern Arduino IDE also has features such as code completion; the reason to try this workflow is the project organization, repeatable settings, and editor tools. See Arduino’s IDE guide.
There are three pieces to understand:
You do not need to install Arduino IDE first. PlatformIO downloads its own tools; changing a board package in Arduino IDE does not change this project’s PlatformIO package. PlatformIO’s Arduino framework documentation explains this setup.

3. Read the project settings
Replace the contents of platformio.ini with:
[env:firebeetle]
platform = platformio/espressif32@8.0.0
board = dfrobot_firebeetle2_esp32e
framework = arduino
monitor_speed = 115200
Save the file. PlatformIO may download packages or refresh its project information.







Line
What it means

A named set of settings. We call this environment firebeetle.

The ESP32 support package and its tools. @8.0.0 selects a specific release.

5. Upload and read the messages

Connect the FireBeetle with the USB data cable.
Close any Arduino IDE Serial Monitor using that board.
Select Upload in the same PlatformIO project tasks, or use the right-arrow icon in its toolbar. Wait for a successful upload.
Select Monitor, or the plug-shaped serial-monitor icon. Confirm it opens at 115200.
You should see alternating messages, and the onboard LED should turn on and off every half second:

LED ON
LED OFF
LED ON
LED OFF
Try changing BLINK_TIME_MS to 1000, save, and upload again. The LED should now spend one second on and one second off. Editing or building alone does not update the program already on the board.

If PlatformIO chooses the wrong port
Open the PlatformIO Core CLI terminal from PlatformIO’s Quick Access → Miscellaneous and run:
pio device list
Compare the list with the board unplugged and plugged in. Windows ports look like COM7; macOS often uses /dev/cu.usbserial-...; Linux often uses /dev/ttyUSB0. Your actual port may differ.
If necessary, add both lines below inside the existing [env:firebeetle] section, replacing COM7 with your board’s port:
upload_port = COM7
monitor_port = COM7
Leave these out when automatic detection works. A teammate’s port will probably differ from yours. See upload options and the serial monitor reference. In the terminal monitor, Ctrl+C exits and releases the port.


The same workflow from a terminal
In the PlatformIO Core CLI terminal, with the project folder as the current directory:

text:
6. Know what belongs in each folder
This is a typical project after its first build. Some folders are created by the wizard or only appear when you need them; the starter ZIP deliberately contains just the essentials.
firebeetle-first-project/
├── platformio.ini       Board, framework, versions, libraries
├── src/
│   └── main.cpp         Your program
├── include/             Your shared .h header files
├── lib/                 Libraries you write for this project
├── test/                Automated tests, when you add them
├── .pio/                Generated builds and downloaded libraries
├── .vscode/             Editor configuration
├── .gitignore           Files Git should leave out
└── README.txt           How to wire, build, and run the project
Start by editing src/main.cpp and platformio.ini. As the code grows, move related functions into additional .cpp files under src/ and put their declarations in .h files under include/.
Treat .pio/ as generated output. Do not edit libraries inside it: your changes can disappear when dependencies are reinstalled. Use lib/ for your own project libraries and lib_deps for published dependencies. The directory reference describes these defaults.
For GitHub, include your source, platformio.ini, .gitignore, and a short README with the wiring and instructions. Keep .pio/ out. The starter also ignores .vscode/; you can later choose to share useful editor settings. If you add a local file such as include/secrets.h for Wi-Fi passwords or service keys, keep it out of Git and share a placeholder example instead.

8. Add Codex or Claude Code
Once your first build and upload work, I recommend trying one AI coding extension. Keeping the assistant beside the project lets you ask about actual files, review changes, and use the build output in the same place. Both options below can help; choose the one you already have access to. AI access and usage limits depend on your account, and neither is required for PlatformIO.

Option A: Codex by OpenAI

In Extensions, find Codex published by OpenAI (openai.chatgpt), using the install link in the official Codex IDE guide.
Open the Codex icon. If it is hidden, use the Command Palette and Codex: Open Codex Sidebar.
Choose Sign in with ChatGPT and finish the browser sign-in. An API-key option also exists, with separate usage-based billing. See OpenAI’s authentication guide.
Keep the FireBeetle project folder open. Open platformio.ini and src/main.cpp, then ask Codex to explain this project before requesting a change.

Use the local project workflow while working with the USB board. Review the changed lines in the editor and build again after accepting an edit.


Option B: Claude Code by Anthropic

Install Claude Code published by Anthropic (anthropic.claude-code) from Extensions.
Open a source file, then click the Claude spark icon or find Claude Code in the Command Palette.
Follow the sign-in prompt. The documented options include a paid Claude subscription or a Claude Console account; check your account’s access and billing.
Reference platformio.ini and src/main.cpp with @ in the conversation, and start with the same explanation request below.

The extension includes the CLI it needs for its chat panel. A separate standalone CLI installation is only needed if you want to run the claude command in a terminal. Follow the official VS Code instructions; on Windows, also check the current Windows prerequisites.


A useful first conversation
Copy this into either assistant:
Read platformio.ini and src/main.cpp. Explain what runs on the computer
and what runs on the FireBeetle 2 ESP32-E. Explain each project setting
and what the LED program does. Do not change any files yet.
Then try one small change:
Replace the delay-based blinking with millis() timing, keeping the same
LED pin and the same 500 ms on / 500 ms off behavior. Print a message only
when the LED changes. Keep the board, framework, and package versions.
Explain the change, then build with pio run -e firebeetle and report the
result. Do not upload; I will test it on the board.
If the assistant cannot find pio, run the build in the PlatformIO Core CLI yourself and give it the first meaningful error and surrounding lines. A build result is more useful than the final line saying “failed.”
Review what changed, upload, and check the LED and messages. Compiling verifies that the code can be built; it does not verify your wiring or prove that a sensor reading is correct. Keep a working Git commit before a larger edit, and leave real passwords and API keys out of prompts and shared files.
For a sensor project, include the exact sensor model, connected GPIO numbers, expected units, and actual error. For example: “My SHT31 uses SDA 21, SCL 22, address 0x44. Explain why this program gets no reading.” The assistant should work from your wiring, not invent it.

The FireBeetle 2 ESP32-E has no onboard debug probe, so stepping through firmware at breakpoints needs additional supported debug hardware and configuration. title: 3  Breadboard
text:
A breadboard is a device used to prototype electronic circuits without the need for soldering. It consists of a plastic board with rows of holes. In the central area, each group of five holes shares a metal strip; the centre gap separates the two groups in each numbered row. Different numbered rows are not connected. Along the sides are power rails marked + and -, typically used for the positive supply and ground. These markings do not supply power: the rails must be wired to a source. Each rail is separate, and some boards split the rails halfway along their length. When a component, such as a resistor, capacitor, or LED, is inserted into a hole on the breadboard, it makes contact with the metal strip that runs underneath the holes, which provides electrical connectivity between the components. This allows multiple components to be connected together to form a circuit. Breadboards are commonly used by hobbyists, students, and engineers to quickly prototype and test electronic circuits before they are soldered onto a printed circuit board.

title: 6  Libraries
text:
6.1 Using the Library Manager
Libraries are a crucial part of working with Arduino boards. They provide pre-written code that can be easily integrated into your own projects, saving time and effort. This guide will walk you through the two main ways of installing libraries in the Arduino IDE: using the Library Manager and manually installing a library downloaded from GitHub.
The Library Manager is the easiest and most straightforward way of installing libraries in the Arduino IDE. Follow these steps:

title: 6  Libraries

10.2 Relay

A relay is an electromagnetic switch that opens and closes circuits electromechanically or electronically. A relatively small electric current that can turn on or off a much larger electric current operates a relay.
The right side in the image above has a set of four pins and a set of three pins. The top set consists of:

VCC should be connected to the ESP32 VCC (5 volts)
GND connects to the ESP32 GND.
IN1 and IN2 are input pins, used to control the bottom and top relays, respectively, and should be connected to a GPIO pin in the ESP32.

The terminals on the left are connected to the load, the equipment that consumes power. The signal you send to the IN pins determines whether the relay is active or not. The relay is triggered when the input goes below about 2V. This means that you’ll have the following scenarios:

Normally Closed (NC) configuration:

HIGH signal – current is flowing
LOW signal – current is not flowing

Normally Open (NO) configuration:

HIGH signal – current is not flowing
LOW signal – current is flowing


Whether you use the NC or NO configuration, you should always connect one of them to the COM (common) terminal.
You should use a normally closed configuration when the current should be flowing most of the time, and you only want to stop it occasionally.
Use a normally open configuration when you want the current to flow occasionally (for example, to turn on a lamp occasionally).

The other set of three pins (on the left in the figure above) are GND, VCC, and JD-VCC. The JD-VCC pin powers the electromagnet of the relay. Notice that the module has a jumper cap connecting the VCC and JD-VCC pins; the one shown here is yellow, but yours may be a different color.
With the jumper cap on, the VCC and JD-VCC pins are connected. That means the relay electromagnet is directly powered from the ESP32 power pin, so the relay module and the ESP32 circuits are not physically isolated from each other.
Without the jumper cap, you need to provide an independent power source to power up the relay’s electromagnet through the JD-VCC pin. That configuration physically isolates the relays from the ESP32 with the module’s built-in optocoupler, which prevents damage to the ESP32 in case of electrical spikes.

The figure above shows in a very simple way that the relay behaves like a switch with respect to the top circuit.

You should NOT build the above circuit, since it is a high voltage circuit (220 V). In class we will use 5, 12 or 24 volts.

text:
11.8 Reading Potentiometer with Analog Pin, convert to angle
Put a piece of cardboard in your potentiometer’s slit. Your goal is to build a calibration curve, that is, a function that converts reading from something you don’t care about (increments from 0 to 4095) to something that you do care about (angle).
The simplest thing you can do is to measure the increments (\(i\)) that you get for two given angles (say, \(\theta\) equals zero and 90 degrees). Let’s say you measured \((i_1,\theta_1)\) and \((i_2,\theta_2)\). If the potentiometer is linear, we will get a linear relationship between angle and increment:
\[
\theta = a i + b
\]
Substitute these two points in the equation above:
\[
\theta_1 = a i_1 + b
\tag{11.1}\]
\[
\theta_2 = a i_2 + b
\tag{11.2}\]
Now let’s subtract Equation 11.2 from Equation 11.1:
\[
\theta_1 - \theta_2 = a (i_1 - i_2)
\tag{11.3}\]
Now solve for the slope \(a\):
\[
a = (\theta_1 - \theta_2) / (i_1 - i_2)
\tag{11.4}\]
To find the intercept \(b\), just substitute \(a\) into Equation 11.1 and solve for \(b\):
\[
b = \theta_1 - a i_1
\tag{11.5}\]

11.9 Voltage divider
Many sensors have calibration curves that relate their resistance changes to the measured variable. For example, the resistance of photoresistors and thermistors changes with light and temperature, respectively. To handle this, we need to understand Voltage Dividers.

Check out this great tutorial
How to derive the equation for the voltage divider?
First, write Ohm’s law for the two components in series:
\[
V_{in} = (R_1 + R_2) I
\tag{11.6}\]
Now write Ohm’s law just for the second component
\[
V_{out} = R_2 I
\tag{11.7}\]
Now solve Equation 11.7 for \(I\)
\[
I = \frac{V_{out}}{R_2}
\tag{11.8}\]
… and substitute it into Equation 11.6:
\[
V_{in} = (R_1 + R_2) \frac{V_{out}}{R_2}
\tag{11.9}\]
Solving for \(V_{out}\) yields the famous equation for the voltage divider:
\[
V_{out} = \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} V_{in}
\tag{11.10}\]
We usually need to find the value of the resistance \(R_2\):
\[
R_2 = R_1 \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in} - V_{out}}
\]
This rearrangement assumes \(R_1 > 0\) and \(0 < V_{out} < V_{in}\), with no load drawing current from the output.

The terminals on the left are connected to the load, the equipment that consumes power. The signal you send to the IN pins determines whether the relay is active or not. The relay is triggered when the input goes below about 2V. This means that you’ll have the following scenarios:

Normally Closed (NC) configuration:

HIGH signal – current is flowing
LOW signal – current is not flowing

Normally Open (NO) configuration:

HIGH signal – current is not flowing
LOW signal – current is flowing


Whether you use the NC or NO configuration, you should always connect one of them to the COM (common) terminal.
You should use a normally closed configuration when the current should be flowing most of the time, and you only want to stop it occasionally.
Use a normally open configuration when you want the current to flow occasionally (for example, to turn on a lamp occasionally).

The other set of three pins (on the left in the figure above) are GND, VCC, and JD-VCC. The JD-VCC pin powers the electromagnet of the relay. Notice that the module has a jumper cap connecting the VCC and JD-VCC pins; the one shown here is yellow, but yours may be a different color.
With the jumper cap on, the VCC and JD-VCC pins are connected. That means the relay electromagnet is directly powered from the ESP32 power pin, so the relay module and the ESP32 circuits are not physically isolated from each other.
Without the jumper cap, you need to provide an independent power source to power up the relay’s electromagnet through the JD-VCC pin. That configuration physically isolates the relays from the ESP32 with the module’s built-in optocoupler, which prevents damage to the ESP32 in case of electrical spikes.
Let’s make an LED blink, but now using a relay. The code below is the same you used to make the LED blink, when it got its energy from pin A4. This time, we will use A4 to signal the relay to open or close the circuit.

Preview — F5: the quick view while editing. Menu: Design → Preview.
Render — F6: calculate the final shape. Wait for it to finish and check the console for errors. Menu: Design → Render.
Export as STL: save the rendered model for the slicer. Menu: File → Export → Export as STL.

On a laptop, the function keys may need Fn. See the OpenSCAD shortcut reference.


Try the workflow

Open OpenSCAD and create a new file.
Type cube([30, 20, 6]); and save it as first-part.scad.
Use Design → Preview (F5) to see a 30 × 20 × 6 mm block. On a laptop, you may need Fn with the function key.
Change 6 to 10 and preview again. You changed its height, not its width or depth.

Preview is for quick editing; Render calculates the final geometry for export. Save both the .scad and .stl files. OpenSCAD’s export instructions.


A few rules that make the code readable
[X, Y, Z] means sideways, front-to-back, and height. A default cube([30,20,6]) starts at the origin [0,0,0]; center=true puts its centre at the origin instead. A cylinder points along Z unless you rotate it.
A shape statement ends in ;. Braces { ... } group shapes. A transformation goes before the shape it changes, without a semicolon between them. // starts a comment. Dimensions and positions can be named variables, such as wall = 2;, instead of repeated numbers.
$fn=64 asks for 64 segments around a circle. It makes round shapes look smoother; it does not change the printer’s layer height. Start with moderate values so previews and STLs stay manageable. The OpenSCAD cheat sheet is a useful reference while reading code.

The operations we use








Operation
In plain language
What to notice




cube(), cylinder(), sphere()
Make a basic solid.
Dimensions, diameter versus radius, and where its origin sits.

Move a shape.
Its dimensions stay the same.

We will solder the class PCB, then try a small open stand. Four raised posts support the board at its mounting holes, leaving room underneath for trimmed component leads. The centre is open so the underside remains accessible.

The holes are not equally inset from all edges. Copying “four holes 4 mm from each corner” would give the wrong locations. In our model, the origin is the bottom-left board corner when viewed from the component side, with X right and Y up.



The printable open stand, with a raised post and screw hole at each mounting position.


View stand + PCB together · Editable stand source · Printable stand STL
The stand has a 3 mm base, 6 mm posts above the base, and 3.4 mm nominal screw holes. Each post widens from an 8 mm top to a 12 mm foot, spreading the load into the frame. This leaves 2.3 mm of plastic around the hole at the top, compared with 1.3 mm in the earlier version. Its overall size is 81.406 × 86.740 × 9 mm. These are design choices you can change in the .scad file. A for loop repeats the same post at each coordinate in the holes list.
The green board in the viewer reproduces the outline, thickness and all 72 drilled holes. It leaves out copper, components, connectors and solder joints. Use it to check the hole pattern; use the real populated PCB to check clearance and access. See the assembled PCB in 3D · Board reference STL · Measured geometry data.






Print a small fit test first



Print the M3 screw-fit test. Starting at its notched end, the holes are 3.2, 3.4 and 3.6 mm in the design. Try your actual M3 screw in each one. Printed holes can come out smaller than drawn, so adjust screw_d in the stand after this test.
Use suitable M3 through-bolts and nuts, preferably nylon around the PCB. These are clearance holes, not printed screw threads; tighten gently rather than driving a screw into the plastic. Choose screw length after measuring the stand, board and fastening hardware together. Check that fasteners and posts clear the solder joints and traces. This is a prototype, not a physically tested fit.


Solder first, mount later. Use a heat-resistant soldering surface. Let the board cool, trim the leads and inspect the joints before fitting the stand. A PLA stand is not a soldering fixture.

From STL to a print in Bambu Studio

Open Bambu Studio and select the printer. Use H2C and the actual installed nozzle diameter. Select the build plate and filament profile that match the lab setup. Begin with a single PLA colour if that is the material the instructor has loaded.
Import the STL, by dragging it onto the plate or using File → Import. Start with screw-fit.stl, then pcb-stand.stl after checking fit. Keep the PCB reference out of the print job.
Check the dimensions. The stand should be about 81.4 × 86.7 × 9 mm at 100% scale. If it is unexpectedly tiny or huge, resolve the units instead of guessing a scale factor. Scaling the whole stand also moves the mounting holes.
Choose the orientation. Put the stand’s broad, flat base on the bed, with the posts pointing up. This design is intended to print in that orientation without supports. Inspect the preview to confirm that every new region has something below it.
Start with a suitable preset. With a 0.4 mm nozzle and ordinary PLA, a 0.20 mm layer-height preset is a reasonable first trial. Use the printer/material preset for temperatures. For this stand, try three walls and roughly 15–20% infill, then inspect the result. These are starting points, not a saved lab profile.
Click Slice plate, then inspect Preview. Move the layer slider from bottom to top. Look for the open window, four posts, clear screw holes, unsupported starts, and unexpected gaps. Read the estimated time and material use. Confirm any support or prime-tower material before printing.
Save the project as .3mf. This keeps your setup for the next iteration. Check the physical plate is clear, confirm the material-to-AMS-slot mapping, and have the instructor check the first job before using Print plate or the lab’s offline transfer method.
Watch the first layer and let the part cool. Keep hands away from the hot nozzle, bed and moving mechanism. Remove the cooled part as demonstrated, try the screw-fit test, and measure before printing more copies.

An AMS slot containing the right colour can still contain the wrong material. Match the material as well. More colours and hotend changes can add time and material use, even with automatic switching. Keep the first exercise simple. Bambu Studio documentation and project links.

section: What to change when a print is disappointing
text:
What to change when a print is disappointing







What you want to improve
What to think about




A smoother curved surface
More curve segments in OpenSCAD, and possibly smaller layers in the slicer. They address different kinds of visible steps.


A stronger bracket
Orientation and wall thickness matter. Layer-to-layer bonding can be the weak direction; more infill alone does not fix everything.


A screw that will not fit
Print a fit test and change that hole diameter in the source. Keep the mounting-hole positions fixed.


An overhang that sags
Reorient the part, change the design, or add suitable supports. Supports take time and may leave marks when removed.


A first layer that does not stick
Check plate cleanliness, plate/material profile and the first layer with the instructor.


A part that fails near heat
Check material suitability. PLA is convenient for first indoor prototypes but can soften near heat; a printed part’s temperature and load limits need checking.



Keep ventilation running as directed in the lab. Ask before trying a new filament type, changing hotends, or altering printer maintenance settings.

section: Working with an LLM on a model
text:
Working with an LLM on a model
Give the LLM as many measured dimensions as you can. Explain what the part must do and what it must fit around. A sketch or photo helps with the overall idea, but include measurements rather than asking it to guess the scale.

Use clear units and a reference point. Give width, depth, height, hole diameters and hole positions, all measured from the same origin.
Describe the real assembly. Include screw heads, nuts, connectors, the switch, cables, solder joints and the space needed to reach them. Say which surfaces may touch and which need clearance.
State what must stay fixed. For example, keep the PCB mounting-hole positions unchanged, keep the top open, and leave enough material around the screws.
Explain how you will print it. Give the material and nozzle size you plan to use. Ask for a sensible orientation, enough wall thickness, and a design that is easy to print and assemble.
Ask for readable, editable code. Use named dimensions, simple shapes and comments. Have it state its assumptions, then change one thing at a time.

There are many ways to make the same part. A shape can be built up from solids, cut out of a larger block, or extruded from a flat outline. Ask for a couple of approaches and compare how easy they are to understand, adjust and print. If a design becomes difficult to work with, describe the problem and try a simpler approach.
Preview and render the result in OpenSCAD, inspect it in the slicer, and check the dimensions against the real components. Start with a small fit test when the design depends on screw holes or tight clearances, then improve it from what you measure.

20.1 Intro
MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport) is a lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol built for low-power devices like the ESP32. We’ll use it to move sensor and control data between our boards and the cloud.

title: 20  MQTT
text:
20.2 Fundamental Concepts

Broker: central hub that routes messages between clients. For class, we use the Hivemq free public broker.
Client: anything that connects to the broker — a sensor, an actuator, or a dashboard. A client can publish, subscribe, or both. For testing, use the Hivemq online client.
Topic: a hierarchical string label for a message (e.g. agriculture/field1/soil_moisture).
Publish / Subscribe: a client publishes a message to a topic; the broker forwards it to every client that subscribed to that topic. Publishers and subscribers never talk to each other directly.

title: 20  MQTT
text:
20.3 A bit more about topics
Think of the broker as a bulletin board. A topic is just the path to a spot on that board — levels separated by /, from general to specific. A publisher pins a note at a precise spot (e.g. agriculture/field2/soil_moisture/30cm); a subscriber reads whichever spot, or group of spots, it cares about.
Here’s that bulletin board for three fields, each tracking temperature, solar radiation, and soil moisture at two depths:

A subscriber can read as narrow or as wide a slice of this board as it needs:

Just field 2’s temperature: agriculture/field2/temperature
Soil moisture at 30 cm, in every field: agriculture/+/soil_moisture/30cm — the + wildcard matches exactly one level, here standing in for the field.
Everything measured in field 1: agriculture/field1/# — the # wildcard matches any number of remaining levels, so it catches both soil-moisture depths too.
Every soil-moisture reading, any field, any depth: agriculture/+/soil_moisture/#

20.4 Let’s try it ourselves
I’ll suggest a few ideas, students will divide themselves in groups of 2, and they can choose what mini project to build:

Upon a button press (digital read), one student’s ESP32 publishes via MQTT a command to “open” or “close”; the other ESP32 subscribes to that topic, and depending on what’s written, opens or closes a relay that powers an LED.
One ESP32 measures temperature and humidity with an SHT31 and publishes the readings every 5 seconds; the other ESP32 subscribes and shows the measurements on an OLED screen.
One ESP32 reads a potentiometer and publishes a 0–255 brightness value; the other subscribes and uses it to dim the built-in RGB LED.
One ESP32 reads a light sensor (photoresistor) and publishes “day” or “night” whenever the light level crosses a threshold; the other subscribes and switches a relay — e.g. a grow light — accordingly.
One ESP32 counts pulses with the pulse sensor and publishes the running count every few seconds; the other subscribes and displays the total on an OLED screen.
One ESP32 reads a touch pin as a doorbell button and publishes a “ring” message; the other subscribes and flashes its RGB LED whenever a ring arrives.

import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt

# MQTT broker details
broker_address = "broker.hivemq.com"
broker_port = 1883

# Callback function when a connection is established with the MQTT broker
def on_connect(client, userdata, flags, rc):
    print("Connected to MQTT broker with result code: " + str(rc))
    # Subscribe to the topic upon successful connection
    client.subscribe("agrotech/mqtt_tutorial/#")

# Callback function when a message is received
def on_message(client, userdata, msg):
    print("Received message: " + str(msg.payload.decode()))

# Create a MQTT client instance
client = mqtt.Client()

# Assign callback functions
client.on_connect = on_connect
client.on_message = on_message

# Connect to the MQTT broker
client.connect(broker_address, broker_port, 60)

# Loop to maintain the connection and process network traffic
client.loop_forever()

import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
import random
import time

# MQTT broker details
broker_address = "broker.hivemq.com"
broker_port = 1883

# Create a MQTT client instance
client = mqtt.Client()

# Connect to the MQTT broker
client.connect(broker_address, broker_port, 60)

temperature = 20.0
# Loop to publish random temperature readings
while True:
    temperature = temperature + random.uniform(-1, 1)  # Generate a random temperature value between 20.0 and 30.0
    client.publish("agrotech/mqtt_tutorial/temperature", str(temperature))  # Publish the temperature value to the topic
    print("Published temperature: " + str(temperature))
    time.sleep(1)  # Wait for 5 seconds before publishing the next temperature reading

# Disconnect from the MQTT broker (not reached in this example)

# Create a DataFrame to store the messages
df = pd.DataFrame(columns=["topic", "value"])

# Callback function when a connection is established with the MQTT broker
def on_connect(client, userdata, flags, rc):
    print("Connected to MQTT broker with result code: " + str(rc))
    # Subscribe to all subtopics within agrotech/mqtt_tutorial/
    client.subscribe("agrotech/mqtt_tutorial/#")

# Callback function when a message is received
def on_message(client, userdata, msg):
    global df
    # Decode the message payload
    value = msg.payload.decode()
    # Extract the subtopic
    subtopic = msg.topic.split("agrotech/mqtt_tutorial/")[1]
    # Get the current time
    timestamp = datetime.now()
    # Create a new DataFrame with the new message
    new_row = pd.DataFrame({"topic": [subtopic], "value": [value]}, index=[timestamp])
    # Append the new row to the DataFrame using concat
    df = pd.concat([df, new_row])
    print(f"Received message on {msg.topic}: {value}")

# Create an MQTT client instance
client = mqtt.Client()

# Assign callback functions
client.on_connect = on_connect
client.on_message = on_message

# Connect to the MQTT broker
client.connect(broker_address, broker_port, 60)

# Loop to maintain the connection and process network traffic
try:
    client.loop_forever()
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    # Save the DataFrame to a CSV file when the script is interrupted
    df.to_csv("mqtt_messages.csv")
    print("Data saved to mqtt_messages.csv")

title: 21  Deep Sleep
text:
21.1 Key Features of Deep Sleep
Deep sleep is a power-saving mode on the ESP32 microcontroller that allows it to significantly reduce its power consumption by shutting down most of its components and functionalities. This mode is particularly useful for battery-powered applications where conserving energy is crucial.

title: 21  Deep Sleep
text:
Low Power Consumption:
Deep sleep drastically reduces the chip’s power use. The current of a complete board also includes its regulators, LEDs and connected sensors.
Preservation of Data:
Variables explicitly placed in RTC (Real-Time Clock) memory can be retained during deep sleep. Waking restarts the application; ordinary RAM and peripheral state are not preserved.
Wake-Up Sources:
The ESP32 can be awakened from deep sleep by various events:

Timer: The internal RTC can be programmed to wake the device after a specified time interval.
External Pin: A change in the state of a designated GPIO pin can trigger a wake-up.
Touch Sensor: Touch pad sensors can be used to wake up the device.
ULP Coprocessor: The Ultra-Low-Power (ULP) coprocessor can run while the main CPU is in deep sleep and trigger a wake-up event based on sensor readings or other conditions.

Application Examples:

Battery-Powered Sensors: Environmental sensors that need to periodically send data can spend most of their time in deep sleep, waking up only to take measurements and transmit data.
IoT Devices: Devices that need to conserve power, such as remote weather stations or smart home devices, can use deep sleep to extend battery life.

title: 28  Psychrometric Chart and Evaporative Cooling
text:
28.2 Evaporative cooling (wiki)
Evaporative coolers lower the temperature of air using the principle of evaporative cooling. Evaporative cooling is the conversion of liquid water into vapor using the thermal energy in the air, resulting in a lower air temperature. The energy needed to evaporate the water is taken from the air in the form of sensible heat, which affects the temperature of the air, and converted into latent heat, the energy present in the water vapor component of the air, whilst the air remains at a constant enthalpy value. This conversion of sensible heat to latent heat is known as an isenthalpic process because it occurs at a constant enthalpy value. Evaporative cooling therefore causes a drop in the temperature of air proportional to the sensible heat drop and an increase in humidity proportional to the latent heat gain. Evaporative cooling can be visualized using a psychrometric chart by finding the initial air condition and moving along a line of constant enthalpy toward a state of higher humidity
In the green house we have an evaporative cooler as shown in this diagram:
 
Water trickles on a celullose pad, then fans push dry air from outside through the pad in which water evaporates and the air gets colder and humidity rises.

section: 28.3 How much can the cooler cool?
text:
28.3 How much can the cooler cool?
The evaporative cooler can cool as low as the “wet bulb trmperature”.
We can look at the chart, and we should for the first time… But let’s calculate it using the PschroLib python package.
All the library’s functions can be found here.
import psychrolib

# Set the unit system, for example to SI (can be either SI or IP) - this needs to be done only once
psychrolib.SetUnitSystem(psychrolib.SI)

altitude = 0
atm_pressure = psychrolib.GetStandardAtmPressure(0)

# Calculate the wet bulb temperature for a dry bulb temperature of 25 C , a relative humidity of 80% and atmospheric pressure (kPa)
WBT = psychrolib.GetTWetBulbFromRelHum(25.0, 0.80,atm_pressure )
print(f'Wet Bulb Temperature: {WBT:.3f} degree C')
print(f'Degrees cooled: {25-WBT:.3f} degree C')
Output:
Wet Bulb Temperature: 22.380 degree C
Degrees cooled: 2.620 degree C
Now let’s see how many degrees will it cool if we have only 30% relative humidity outside:
WBT = psychrolib.GetTWetBulbFromRelHum(25.0, 0.30,atm_pressure )
print(f'Wet Bulb Temperature: {WBT:.3f} degree C')
print(f'Degrees cooled: {25-WBT:.3f} degree C')
Output:
Wet Bulb Temperature: 14.422 degree C
Degrees cooled: 10.578 degree C
As you can see it is much more efficient in dry areas like deserts. Therefore it is many times called a “desert cooler”. What will the relative humidity be for the air that leaves the pad?

28.3.1 Efficiency
Theoretically, an evaporative cooler cools down to the wet bulb temperature, but in reality it is not 100% efficient and the air comes out not as cold. Many factors can influence: water quality, air speed, pad thickness, pad condition (you will se that ours is not great…), etc. We can calculate the efficiency by this equation:
\[
\eta = \dfrac{T_i-T_o}{T_i-T_w},
\]
where

\(T_i = \:\) temperature coming into the pad.

\(T_o = \:\) temperature coming out of the pad.
\(T_w = \:\) wet bulb temperature.

We can calculate it using data from our sensors and learn about the greenhouse we are using.
For example:
If we measure 30C and 60% humidity outside and the temperature out of the pad is 26C
T_i = 30
T_o = 26
T_w = psychrolib.GetTWetBulbFromRelHum(T_i, 0.60,atm_pressure )
print(f'Wet Bulb Temperature: {T_w:.3f} degree C')

effi = (T_i-T_o)/(T_i-T_w)
print(f'Efficiency is: {100*effi:.3f} %')
Output:
Wet Bulb Temperature: 23.812 degree C
Efficiency is: 64.646 %


28.3.2 What else can we calculate?
Knowing the fan’s capacity (we can measure that too using wind sensors) and the temerature and humidity of the air leaving the greenhouse we can calculate:

Amount of water evaporated from the pad,
Amount of water evaporated from the greenhouse (being a concreete greenhouse that means total evaporation from plants and pots),
Heat removed from the greenouse by the flowing air,

These are just some ideas, you can think of other interesting things to calculate.
There are existing models for predicting the temperatures of greenhouses. There are many other factors taking place such as solar radiation, outside wind, amounts of plants in the greenhouse, etc. We won’t be studying those here, but maybe you can come up with some models/conclusions/correlations of your own :)

text:
37.1 Updates
In the last month of the semester you will pair up with another student to do your Final Project. This project is an opportunity for you to apply all what we learned, to be inovative, and create your own agrotech project. You will have a few weeks to plan, setup and run your projects. At the end of the semester we will have a festive presentation day in which each pair of students will present their projects.
Please consult this Google Spreadsheet to be up-to-date with what’s going on with the various projects. Every team should update this spreadsheet regularly with the relevant information.

title: 37  Final Project
text:
37.2 The platform
This year the final projects will all take place in a greenhouse on campus and will share the theme of data logging and control. Each team’s project will involve irrigation control based on sensor readings (see minimal requirements below), and will include an expansion in whatever way the group finds useful and fun.

Minimal requirements:

set up environmental sensors, such as temperature, humidity, soil moisture, wind, radiation, etc.
log all the measured data in a dedicated Thingspeak channel.
set up an irrigation control system based on the sensed data.

Extra: something cool or creative to add to this basic setup, for example

extra sensors
graphical user interface such as screen with menus and buttons
calculations based on measurements, such as the Penman equation, using python
optimization of water usage
fertilization through irrigation (fertigation)
alerts in case something malfunctions
consult with the lecturers regarding other ideas

title: 37  Final Project
text:
37.3 Final Report = GitHub page
Documenting your project well is probably one of the most important lessons you will learn. Without documentation your projects will not live on and they will end their life right after the semester is over; you will forget what exactly you did and no one will be able to reproduce what you have done. We don’t want that for our projects…
The goal of the Agrotech-Lab course is to create a repository of all the cool projects made over the years. That way the projects will live forever and future students and other people around the world can learn from your work.
We require that each team creates a Github page including all the documentation. It should include:

Introduction: general explanation about the project and its goals
Hardware and assembly: Make the description as detailed as posible. Include many photos, links to order, datasheets etc.
Code: Provide all code used in this project. Code should be organized with comments throughout explaining it.
Instructions: How to make and use the project.
Experiment: Show an example of the project “in action”.

Plese note, the github page is your “final project paper/report”.

title: 37  Final Project
text:
37.4 Presentation
On the last day, when we meet to show our projects, each team will give a short talk of 5 minutes. During this talk you will touch the following points:

What did you do?
Why do a project like yours?
Are there agricultural or other benefits?
How did you do it? Hardware and code (no need to go over it, just explain in general).
What did you learn? Show graphs and data analysis.


37.4.1 Attention!
Presentation is something you present to others, it does not mean a “Powerpoint presentation”. Your presentation will be solely based on your GitHub repository.

40.1 MQTT in the greenhouse (how control & sensing works)
In the greenhouse we use MQTT as a lightweight “message bus” that lets devices publish sensor data and receive control commands.
Why MQTT?

title: 40  MQTT in project greenhouse
text:
One broker, many devices: sensors and controllers don’t need to know about each other directly—everything goes through the broker.
Safer control: students don’t need to wire high-voltage loads or power electronics. The high-voltage / high-current parts (e.g., irrigation solenoids, pumps, fans) are already installed and protected (relays, fuses, enclosures, labeling).
Faster labs: you focus on data + logic + automation, not on dangerous wiring.

40.3 MQTT basics you need for this course

40.3.1 Topics
A topic is a string path (like folders). Devices publish messages to topics; other devices subscribe to topics.
Example control topic:

/greenhouse/outside/irrigation/solenoid5



40.3.2 Payloads
For most greenhouse actuators we use a simple convention:

0 → OFF / closed
1 → ON / open

So publishing 1 to a solenoid topic opens that valve; publishing 0 closes it.

41.1 Intro
Each FireBeetle board connects to Wi-Fi and subscribes to an MQTT topic. Whenever a new message is published to the topic, the board receives it and changes the color of its built-in RGB LED accordingly.

The board listens to the following topic:

You can publish messages to this topic using an MQTT client, such as the MQTTX Web Client. Make sure to connect to the broker broker.emqx.io on port 1883.

You can send color commands in various formats:

17  Soldering and Wires
text:
17.2 Using an Arduino Nano ESP32
You can use the same class PCB with an Arduino Nano ESP32. Put the Nano on a breadboard beside the PCB and run ten jumper wires to the empty FireBeetle connections. The sensors, button and LEDs stay on the class PCB.






Use the Nano ESP32 and 3.3 V



This wiring is for the Arduino Nano ESP32, not the classic 5 V Arduino Nano. Power the Nano through USB-C and connect its 3V3 output to the PCB’s 3V3 connection, with a shared GND. Keep VUSB/VBUS, VIN and 5 V away from the PCB’s 3V3 and signal connections. The Nano ESP32 uses 3.3 V signals; see the Arduino power specifications.



17.2.1 Set up the boards

Unplug power and remove the FireBeetle. The Nano has a different pin layout: do not plug it into the FireBeetle sockets. Leave the FireBeetle disconnected throughout this setup.
Place the Nano across the breadboard’s centre gap, with its two rows of pins on opposite sides. Each Nano pin goes into a separate connected strip of five breadboard holes. Leave the USB connector accessible. If your Nano has no headers, solder male headers onto it first.
Choose the jumper ends that fit your PCB. For female sockets on the PCB, use male-to-male jumper wires. For male pins on the PCB, use male-to-female jumpers, with the female end on the PCB. The breadboard end is male in either case. Empty, unsoldered PCB holes need soldered headers before you can use push-in jumpers reliably.
Run each jumper from a free hole in the Nano pin’s connected strip to the PCB contact in the table. Keep the wires short enough to follow easily; red for 3V3 and black for GND help. The PCB already contains the sensor divider resistors and LED resistors, so you do not need to duplicate those circuits on the breadboard.

If the breadboard connections are unfamiliar, try the breadboard explorer first.


17.2.2 Find the right PCB contacts
Look at the component side, with the plant logo and SHT31 at the top, and the OLED, button and LEDs at the bottom. The FireBeetle’s USB end would point left. The upper FireBeetle row has 14 small contacts; the lower row has 18. Count from the left separately in each row, skipping the larger mounting holes. These row positions are only a way to find the holes; they are not GPIO numbers.



The empty FireBeetle socket area, viewed from the component side. Use upper-row contacts 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 and 8, and lower-row contacts 12, 13, 15 and 16.


Open the socket diagram at full size.
Follow the labels printed on the Nano, using the official Nano ESP32 pinout to locate them. The PCB destinations below were traced through our KiCad design.

The OLED and SHT31 share the PCB’s I²C bus: one SDA wire and one SCL wire serve both modules. Leave all other FireBeetle contacts unconnected. Check the row positions and 3V3/GND connections before plugging the Nano’s USB cable in.


17.2.3 Use the Nano pin names in your code
In Arduino IDE, install Arduino ESP32 Boards by Arduino from Boards Manager, then select Arduino Nano ESP32 as your board. In Arduino IDE, use Tools → Pin Numbering → By Arduino pin (default). Write pin labels such as D6, D7, A2 and A3 in your sketch instead of copying bare ESP32 GPIO numbers from a FireBeetle example. The labels also work if the Nano’s pin-numbering setting changes; Arduino explains the two numbering options here.
const int THERMISTOR_PIN = A2;
const int LIGHT_PIN = A3;
const int BUTTON_PIN = D7;
const int LED_PINS[] = {D6, D3, D2};  // PCB LEDs D1, D2, D3

// Use these definitions in the complete check sketch linked below.
For I²C, include <Wire.h> and call Wire.begin() inside setup(). With the Nano ESP32 board selected, this uses SDA = A4 and SCL = A5.
Adapt older examples to this wiring. On this PCB the thermistor is on A2 and the photoresistor is on A3, even if a standalone lesson uses A4. Here A4 is already SDA. Replace explicit FireBeetle I²C GPIO choices with Wire.begin() when using this Nano setup. A PCB label like “D1” beside an LED is the component’s name; it does not mean Nano pin D1.


17.2.4 Check the connections
Download the complete Nano ESP32 PCB check sketch. Open it in Arduino IDE, select your Nano ESP32 and port, upload, then open Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. It uses only the built-in Arduino and Wire libraries.

Press and release the button: all three PCB LEDs should turn on while it is pressed and off when released. A pressed button reads LOW because it connects D7 to ground.
Cover and uncover the photoresistor: the Light A3 reading should change. Gently warm the thermistor between your fingers and watch Thermistor A2 change. These are raw 12-bit readings (0–4095), not lux or degrees; temperature conversion needs the actual thermistor and resistor values.
Watch the I²C scan every five seconds: with both modules installed and powered, expect two responding addresses. This check finds the OLED and SHT31 on the bus; it does not draw on the screen or read temperature yet. If none appear, check the shared power, ground, SDA and SCL wiring. If only one appears, check the other module’s solder joints and pin order.

Once these checks work, use the OLED lesson and digital-sensor lesson, keeping the Nano pin choices above.
